title: Observability for Agent Workflows
summary: After completing this intermediate module, you can design observable records for an agent workflow and use them to reconstruct execution, distinguish evidence from inference, and locate a failed step. These are capabilities you may not have had before completing the module.
objectives: Design event records that connect each workflow step to its request and parent step.
Reconstruct an agent workflow as an ordered sequence of recorded events.
Use recorded outcomes and timing information to locate failures, retries, and delays.
Distinguish facts present in observability records from conclusions that require further evidence.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes you understand that an agent workflow consists of multiple software steps, but it does not assume experience with a particular provider or observability implementation.

Observability records help an operator examine what a workflow did after or while it ran. The goal is not merely to collect isolated messages. The goal is to preserve enough context to connect events, reconstruct execution, and identify where observed behavior diverged from the expected path.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous cited source, content/modules/reliable-agent-workflows/agent-observability.json, was an unregistered publisher entry and had never been verified. It was not a resolvable HTTPS source, so it was replaced with the official sources listed at the end of this module.

The source correction affects the support for two parts of the module: managing event records across their lifecycle and correlating related work across process boundaries. The correlation guidance now follows the cited trace-context standard's model of a shared trace identity and a parent relationship. This currency correction does not change the module's provider-neutral scope.

sections.title: Record useful workflow events
paragraphs: Treat each significant workflow step as an event that can be connected to the larger execution. A useful record identifies the workflow execution, identifies the step, states the event type and observed outcome, records when the event occurred, and preserves the relationship to the step that initiated it.

Record both successful and unsuccessful outcomes. A failure record without the preceding steps may reveal where execution stopped but not how it reached that point. Conversely, success-only records can hide retries, fallback paths, and intermediate failures.

Event records have a lifecycle. They are generated, transmitted, stored, analyzed, and eventually disposed of. The cited log-management guidance treats these activities as connected responsibilities rather than unrelated tasks.

sections.title: Correlate related work
paragraphs: An agent workflow can cross process or service boundaries. Preserve a shared trace identity as work crosses those boundaries so that records from the same execution can be grouped. Preserve parent relationships so that a learner or operator can determine which step initiated another step.

A shared identity answers which events belong to the same execution. A parent relationship answers how those events are connected. Both are needed when concurrent branches produce events whose timestamps overlap.

The cited trace-context standard defines a common mechanism for passing trace identity and relationship information between distributed components. This module uses the standard's general correlation model without requiring a particular implementation.

sections.title: Reconstruct and diagnose execution
paragraphs: Begin diagnosis by grouping records that share the same workflow identity. Order the records using their recorded timing and parent relationships, then compare the reconstructed path with the expected sequence of steps.

Look for a step that started without a recorded completion, an unsuccessful outcome, repeated attempts, or an unusually long recorded duration. These observations locate where further investigation should begin. They do not, by themselves, prove the underlying cause.

Keep observed facts separate from inferences. For example, a record showing that a step timed out is evidence of the timeout. A conclusion that network congestion caused it is an inference unless additional evidence supports that conclusion.
sections.callout: Observability can establish only what the recorded evidence supports. Missing records must not be treated as proof that an event did not occur.

sections.title: Apply the method
paragraphs: For a new workflow, identify the significant steps and the possible parent-child relationships before deciding what to record. Ensure that each significant event can be associated with one workflow execution and, when applicable, with the step that initiated it.

For an existing workflow, select one execution and attempt to reconstruct it using only its records. If you cannot determine event membership, ordering, parentage, or outcome, the missing information identifies a concrete observability gap.

After this module, you can turn a collection of disconnected events into a correlation plan, reconstruct a recorded execution, and state which conclusions are supported by evidence and which remain inferences.

questions.prompt: Which information best supports reconstruction of parent-child relationships when a workflow crosses process boundaries?
choices: A shared trace identity together with parent relationships
A count of all successful workflows
A list of event messages without workflow identity
The total storage used by all records
questions.explanation: The module explains that a shared trace identity groups events from one execution, while parent relationships show how its steps are connected.

questions.prompt: Why is recording only a final failure insufficient for reconstructing a workflow?
choices: It prevents the failure from having a timestamp.
It may omit the preceding steps and context that led to the failure.
It proves that no retry occurred.
It automatically removes the workflow identity.
questions.explanation: The module states that a failure record without preceding steps may show where execution stopped but not how it reached that point.

questions.prompt: A record states that a workflow step timed out. Which conclusion is directly supported by that record alone?
choices: A parent step supplied invalid data.
questions.explanation: The timeout is the observed fact. Claims about its cause remain inferences until additional evidence supports them.
